Article.ArticleTitle: Ultrasound-Guided Pudendal Nerve Block in Elderly Pelvic Organ Prolapse Surgery: Impact on Anesthetic Consumption and Postoperative Recovery-A Randomized Clinical Trial.

Abstract.AbstractText: Nerve block is often used for multimodal analgesia. Surgeries for pelvic organ prolapse (POP) in elderly patients are focused on the perineal area, where pudendal nerve block (PNB) can provide analgesia or anaesthesia. There are limited studies on PNB in POP surgery, mainly addressing postoperative pain relief. This prospective randomized controlled trial examined the impact of ultrasound-guided PNB on intraoperative medication and postoperative recovery in elderly POP surgery patients.

Patients aged 60-70 undergoing total vaginal hysterectomy (with or without sacral fixation/colporrhaphy) under general anesthesia were randomized into two groups: PNB (pudendal nerve block) and NPNB (no pudendal nerve block). Anesthesia was induced with target-controlled infusions of remifentanil (3 ng/mL) and propofol (3 µg/mL). The study compared intraoperative anesthetic doses, hemodynamic changes, cardiovascular drug needs, wakefulness time, and post-op recovery quality between the groups.

58 patients completed the study. The PNB group required significantly less remifentanil (386.6 ± 239.1 µg vs 563.1 ± 235.7 µg, p = 0.005) and propofol (645.5 ± 315.2 mg vs 804.2 ± 297.2 mg, p = 0.028) compared to the NPNB group. Intraoperative hemodynamics were more stable in the PNB group, with a reduced need for vasopressors. The PNB group also exhibited faster emergence, lower postoperative pain, and less oversedation,with a non-significant trend toward higher QoR-40 scores.

Ultrasound-guided PNB in elderly POP surgery patients reduced opioid and anesthetic doses, shortened awakening time, and produced clinically favourable improvements in postoperative recovery. Larger studies are needed to confirm these benefits for postoperative rehabilitation.

Article.ArticleTitle: Effect of Different Single-Session Durations of Intermittent Pneumatic Compression on the Prevention of Deep Vein Thrombosis in Postoperative ICU Patients: A Randomized Controlled Trial.

Abstract.AbstractText: BACKGROUND Deep vein thrombosis (DVT) is a common and potentially life-threatening complication in postoperative ICU patients. Intermittent pneumatic compression (IPC) is widely used for mechanical thromboprophylaxis; however, the optimal single-session duration of IPC remains unclear. This randomized controlled trial aimed to evaluate the efficacy of different single-session durations of IPC for preventing DVT in postoperative ICU patients. MATERIAL AND METHODS This prospective randomized controlled trial enrolled 138 patients who were randomized into 3 groups (n = 46 each) receiving IPC 3 times daily, with single-session durations of 40 minutes, 2 hours, or 6 hours. DVT incidence, coagulation parameters (D-dimer [mg/L] and fibrinogen [FIB; g/L]), and adverse events were compared on postoperative days 3 and 5. RESULTS Baseline characteristics were comparable among groups (P>0.05). The 6-hour group had a DVT incidence of 0% on both days, significantly lower than those in the 40-minute (15.21% and 32.61%) and 2-hour (8.70% and 34.78%) groups (P<0.05). No significant intergroup differences in D-dimer levels were observed (P>0.05); FIB levels significantly differed only on day 3 (P<0.05). Adverse events occurred in 6 patients (13.04%) in the 6-hour group, whereas none occurred in the other 2 groups. CONCLUSIONS Although 6-hour single-session IPC provides the most effective DVT prevention, it is associated with a higher risk of skin-related adverse events. Shorter, more frequent IPC (40 minutes or 2 hours per session, 3 times daily) may represent a preferable strategy for postoperative ICU patients due to its balance of efficacy, safety, and clinical feasibility.

Article.ArticleTitle: Photo- and Temperature-Conditioned Versus Conventional Platelet-Rich Plasma for Androgenetic Alopecia: A Split-Scalp, Double-Blind, and Randomized Active-Comparator Trial.

Abstract.AbstractText: Androgenetic alopecia (AGA) is a progressive hair disorder characterized by follicular miniaturization and gradual reductions in hair density and hair shaft diameter. Platelet-rich plasma (PRP) has emerged as a regenerative therapeutic modality for AGA. Experimental literature suggests that physical conditioning may influence platelet activation and the release of platelet-derived mediators. However, whether combined red-light and low-temperature conditioning of PRP provides additional clinical benefit in AGA has not been investigated. This study therefore compared photo- and temperature-conditioned platelet-rich plasma (PTC-PRP), prepared using red-light exposure under low-temperature conditions, with conventional PRP (C-PRP) in patients with AGA.

This split-scalp, double-blind randomized active-comparator trial enrolled 21 adults with mild-to-moderate AGA. Each participant received four intradermal treatment sessions at 4-week intervals. One randomized scalp side received PTC-PRP, while the contralateral side received C-PRP. Trichoscopic assessments were performed at baseline and Weeks 4, 8, 12, 16, and 24. Outcomes included hair density, non-vellus hair density, and non-vellus hair diameter. Pain scores and adverse events were recorded.

Longitudinal improvements from baseline were observed for several trichoscopic outcomes on both treatment sides. However, treatment-by-time interactions were not significant for hair density (p = 0.966), non-vellus hair density (p = 0.869), or non-vellus hair diameter (p = 0.627). Post hoc baseline-adjusted comparisons, three-way treatment-by-time-by-sex interactions, and sensitivity analyses excluding two stable topical-minoxidil users were also nonsignificant. No serious adverse events were observed, and both treatments were well tolerated.

Both C-PRP and PTC-PRP were associated with increases in hair shaft diameter over 24 weeks, while improvements in hair density were modest and variable. No statistically significant efficacy or tolerability difference was detected between PTC-PRP and C-PRP.

Article.ArticleTitle: Two-year randomized clinical evaluation of catechin doped in a universal adhesive on non-carious cervical lesions restorations.

Abstract.AbstractText: This randomized, blinded clinical trial evaluated the 24-month clinical performance of a universal adhesive (Single Bond Universal) containing 0.1 wt% epigallocatechin-3-gallate (EGCG) for the restoration of non-carious cervical lesions (NCCLs using self-etch and etch-and-rinse strategies.

A total of 160 restorations were placed in 29 patients and randomly allocated to four groups: etch-and-rinse (ER), etch-and-rinse with EGCG (ER-EGCG), self-etch (SE), and self-etch with EGCG (SE-EGCG). EGCG was directly incorporated into the adhesive, which was applied according to the manufacturer's instructions. All lesions were restored with a nanofilled composite resin (Filtek Z350XT) and evaluated at baseline and after 6, 12, 18, and 24 months according to the World Dental Federation criteria. Data were analyzed using the Kruskal-Wallis and McNemar tests (α = 0.05).

Participant recall rates were 100% at baseline and 6 months, and 93.1%, 89.7%, and 72.4% at 12, 18, and 24 months, respectively. No significant differences were observed among groups for any evaluated clinical criterion throughout the 24-month follow-up (p > 0.05). At 24 months, retention rates were 90% for SE and SE-EGCG and 100% for ER and ER-EGCG. No significant differences were observed between baseline and 24-month evaluations within any group (p > 0.05). Incorporation of 0.1 wt% EGCG into the universal adhesive did not compromise the clinical performance of NCCL restorations over 24 months, regardless of the bonding strategy.
Incorporation of 0.1 wt% EGCG into a universal adhesive did not affect the clinical performance of NCCL restorations over 24 months.

Incorporation of 0.1 wt% EGCG into a universal adhesive did not improve the clinical performance of NCCL restorations over 24 months compared with the unmodified adhesive. However, EGCG incorporation did not adversely affect restoration performance when the adhesive was used with either etch-and-rinse or self-etch strategies.

Article.ArticleTitle: Exosome-based topical formulations as adjuncts to fractional Nd: YAG laser for postoperative facial scars.

Abstract.AbstractText: Commercial topical formulations marketed as exosome skin boosters are increasingly used as adjuncts to laser treatment, but their additional benefit for postoperative facial scars remains uncertain. This randomized controlled trial allocated 150 patients to fractional 1064-nm Nd laser treatment followed by a control hydrogel, a human-derived formulation, or a plant-derived formulation (50 per group). Five treatment sessions were performed at 2-week intervals. Outcomes were assessed at baseline and 2 weeks after the final session using the modified Vancouver Scar Scale (mVSS), patient and observer components of the Patient and Observer Scar Assessment Scale (POSAS), and grayscale intensity (GSI) quantified from Mark-Vu images using ImageJ. Eleven participants were lost to follow-up, leaving 139 participants in the complete-case analysis: 46, 47, and 46 in the respective groups. Both adjunctive formulation groups showed significantly greater reductions in mVSS, observer POSAS, and GSI than the control group. Patient POSAS improved over time but did not demonstrate a significant time × group interaction. No statistically significant difference was detected between the human-derived and plant-derived formulations; equivalence was not established. No serious adverse events were reported during the observed period. Adjunctive formulations were associated with additional short-term improvements in clinician-rated scar outcomes and an exploratory optical measure, without a demonstrated additional patient-reported benefit. These findings apply to the complete formulations and do not establish an exosome-specific effect, sustained scar remodeling, or long-term safety.

Journal.Title: Supportive care in cancer : official journal of the Multinational Association of Supportive Care in Cancer

Article.ArticleTitle: Changes in functional capacity, flexibility and depressive symptoms in women with breast cancer submitted to adjuvant radiotherapy: randomized controlled clinical trial with mat pilates.

Abstract.AbstractText: To evaluate the impact of Mat Pilates on functional capacity, flexibility, and depressive symptoms in women diagnosed with breast cancer who received adjuvant radiotherapy.

In this randomized clinical trial, 164 women with breast cancer (stages 0-III), aged 18 years or older, were randomized, and 156 were included in the analyses (79 in the Mat Pilates group and 77 in the control group). Handgrip strength, functional exercise capacity assessed by the 2-Minute Step Test (2MST), flexibility, and depressive symptoms were evaluated at baseline, at the end of radiotherapy (RT), and at 30 days, 3 months, and 6 months after RT. Generalized estimating equations (GEE) were used to analyze functional capacity and flexibility, while the cumulative incidence of new depressive symptoms was estimated among participants without depressive symptoms at baseline.

No significant group × time interactions were observed for handgrip strength (Wald χ2 = 7.834; df = 4; p = 0.098), the 2-Minute Step Test (Wald χ2 = 6.877; df = 4; p = 0.143), or flexibility (Wald χ2 = 3.728; df = 4; p = 0.444). During the RT period, the cumulative of new depressive symptoms was 14.8%.

Functional capacity and flexibility improved over time, but their trajectories did not differ significantly between the Mat Pilates and control groups. No significant between-group difference was observed in the cumulative incidence of new depressive symptoms.

Article.ArticleTitle: Short-term physiological responses to nocturnal pressurization in male high-altitude workers: an exploratory pilot randomized controlled trial.

Abstract.AbstractText: This exploratory pilot randomized controlled trial investigated whether a nocturnal pressurization intervention, designed to simulate altitude reduction during sleep, was associated with changes in multi-system physiological responses in male workers with chronic intermittent high-altitude exposure.

Twenty-four male workers were randomized to a Pressurization group (n = 12) or a control group (n = 12); Over a 5-week protocol, the Pressurization group slept at the simulated altitudes while both groups worked at 3500 m. The primary outcome was mean nocturnal peripheral oxygen saturation (SpO2); secondary outcomes were ambulatory blood pressure (BP), serum normetanephrine and metanephrine, Renin-Angiotensin-Aldosterone System components, and oxidative stress markers.

The intervention was associated with short-term changes, the largest of which occurred during the 2000 m-simulated week. SpO2 was higher than in controls at 2500 m and 2000 m (both p < 0.001). Nocturnal diastolic BP was lower at 2500 m (- 7.25 mmHg, p = 0.024), normetanephrine, metanephrine and angiotensin II were reduced at 2000 m (Ang II: -23.10 pg/mL, p = 0.011), and 8-iso-PGF2α was lower with higher total antioxidant capacity at both altitudes. None of these differences persisted at the fifth-week recovery assessment.

A nocturnal pressurization intervention simulating descent to 2000 m was associated with improved nocturnal oxygenation and short-term reductions in neurohormonal and oxidative stress in male high-altitude workers. The changes were reversible and had disappeared one week after the intervention ceased; they should therefore not be interpreted as an improvement in long-term adaptation, and the study should be regarded as hypothesis-generating.

Article.ArticleTitle: Effects of Cooking With Liquefied Petroleum Gas or Biomass on Lung Function Among Pre-School Aged Children in Peru: A Prospective Follow-Up of a Randomized Trial.

Abstract.AbstractText: Billions worldwide are exposed to household air pollution (HAP) from solid fuel use, increasing risk of lung function impairment and chronic respiratory disease. Understanding HAP effects on early life lung function may identify critical windows for intervention.

We performed respiratory oscillometry in 3-5-year-olds whose mothers participated in a randomized trial of LPG versus usual solid fuel use during pregnancy and infancy. We assessed resistance (R7) and reactance (X7) at 7 Hertz, frequency dependence of resistance (R7-19), resonance frequency (fres) and area above the reactance curve from 7 Hertz (AX7). We computed z-scores for R7, X7, fres, and AX7 from pediatric reference equations. Rigorous quality control was applied. Exposure-response analyses examined the association between R7 or AX7 z-scores and prenatal or postnatal PM2.5 or CO exposures.

We tested 101 children (mean [±SD] age 4.4 ± 0.6 years, 51.5% male, 50.5% intervention). Mean R7, X7, fres and AX7 z-scores were similar between intervention and control groups: -0.1 ± 1.0 vs -0.2 ± 1.2, -0.8 ± 1.0 vs -1.0 ± 1.1, 0.9 ± 1.1 vs 0.4 ± 1.1, and 1.2 ± 1.0 vs 1.3 ± 1.3, respectively. Intention-to-treat analysis showed no differences between arms in pre-bronchodilator lung function or bronchodilator response, except for a larger post-bronchodilator decrease in mean fres z-score in the intervention arm (-0.36, 95% CI -0.71 to -0.02). Postnatal CO exposure was associated with higher AX7 z-scores, indicating worse reactance (0.041 per 1 ppm CO increase, 95% CI 0.003 to 0.078). No associations were found for PM2.5 exposure.

Early-life LPG use did not improve oscillometric lung function compared with those exposed to biomass smoke. An exploratory association between postnatal CO exposure and impaired lung reactance warrants confirmation in larger cohorts.

Journal.Title: Research and practice in thrombosis and haemostasis

Article.ArticleTitle: Clinical outcomes, anticoagulation practice patterns, and quality of life after cancer-associated pulmonary embolism: secondary outcomes of the Hydra randomized clinical trial.

Abstract.AbstractText: Despite its high prevalence, practice-based data on management and outcomes after cancer-associated pulmonary embolism (PE) are scarce, and no studies have investigated quality of life.
We aimed to evaluate clinical outcomes, anticoagulation practice patterns, and quality of life after cancer-associated PE.

The Hydra randomized clinical trial assessed the safety of the YEARS algorithm versus computed tomography pulmonary angiography only to exclude acute PE in patients with cancer. Patients with PE at baseline or during 90-day follow-up were included in this study. Outcomes were recurrent venous thromboembolism, major bleeding, all-cause mortality, anticoagulation practice patterns, and quality of life as assessed by the Pulmonary Embolism Quality of Life (PEmb-QoL) questionnaire. PEmb-QoL scores were compared with those for the general PE population reported in the FOCUS study. Lower scores indicate better QoL.

A total of 125 patients were included, of which 103 (82%) had PE at baseline, and 22 (18%) developed PE during follow-up. The 90-day cumulative incidence of recurrent venous thromboembolism and major bleeding was 2.5% (95% CI 0.67%-6.6%) and 2.5% (95% CI 0.68%-6.7%), respectively. All-cause mortality at 90 days was 32% (95% CI 23%-40%). Two-thirds of patients continued anticoagulation until less than 24 hours before death, and the median time between stopping anticoagulation and death was 10 days (IQR, 4-14). The median 90-day PEmb-QoL score was 33% (IQR, 13-51) versus 20% (IQR, 10-40) reported in the FOCUS study.
Patients with cancer-associated PE suffer from high mortality, high morbidity, and impaired quality of life. Anticoagulation therapy is frequently continued until the last days of life.

Article.ArticleTitle: Therapy onset and characteristics associated with improvement following HABIT-ILE in infants with unilateral cerebral palsy: secondary analysis of a randomized controlled trial.

Abstract.AbstractText: To explore the association between therapy onset and changes in motor and functional outcomes and identify characteristics associated with greater changes in infants with unilateral cerebral palsy (UCP) following Hand-Arm Bimanual Intensive Therapy-Including Lower Extremities (HABIT-ILE).

This study included 38 infants aged 6 to 20 months (mean = 14.4 ± 4.3 months) with UCP. All received 50 h of HABIT-ILE and were assessed pre-intervention and 3 months later. Outcomes included Mini-Assisting Hand Assessment (Mini-AHA; primary), Gross Motor Function Measure-66 (GMFM-66) and Canadian Occupational Performance Measure (COPM). Regression analyses explored changes in outcomes in relation to age at therapy onset, prematurity, type and side of lesion, and baseline motor abilities.

Age at therapy onset was not significantly associated with changes in Mini-AHA or COPM satisfaction scores. However, younger age was associated with larger changes in the GMFM-66 and the COPM performance scores. Regarding baseline characteristics associated with greater improvement, the baseline GMFM-66 score was associated with changes in GMFM-66.

These exploratory analyses found that younger age at therapy initiation was associated with larger changes in GMFM-66 and COPM performance scores, suggesting that early therapy onset may be associated with greater improvements in gross motor and functional performance. Baseline gross motor abilities were also associated with changes following HABIT-ILE, suggesting that these characteristics may contribute to variability in observed changes and warrant further investigation in larger studies.

Article.ArticleTitle: Ciprofol-Based Total Intravenous Anesthesia During Pediatric Laparoscopic Surgery: A Double-Blind, Randomized Controlled, Non-Inferiority Clinical Trial.

Abstract.AbstractText: This double-blind, randomized controlled trial evaluated whether ciprofol is non-inferior to propofol as the primary agent for total intravenous anesthesia (TIVA) in pediatric laparoscopic surgery, with respect to extubation time and safety profile.

Children aged 2-12 years (ASA I-II) undergoing laparoscopic surgery were randomly assigned (1:1) to receive either ciprofol or propofol for TIVA. The primary outcome was time to extubation, with a predefined non-inferiority margin (Δ) of 4.8 minutes. Secondary outcomes included recovery metrics, emergence delirium, pain scores, hemodynamic profiles, and safety indicators.

A total of 86 children (43 per group) were enrolled. Extubation time was 17.3±4.9 min in the ciprofol group and 20.1±4.9 min in the propofol group (mean difference, -2.79 min; 95% CI, -4.9 to -0.7). The upper bound of the 95% CI (-0.73 min) was well below the non-inferiority margin of 4.8 min, confirming non-inferiority (one-sided P < 0.0001). Anesthesia and surgery times, recovery metrics, and pain scores did not differ significantly between groups. The incidence of emergence delirium was similar (7.0% vs 2.3%, P=0.616). In exploratory analyses, individuals in the ciprofol group seemed to have overall higher systolic, diastolic, and mean blood pressure than those in the propofol group, while heart rate did not differ between the two groups.

Ciprofol was non-inferior to propofol for extubation time in pediatric TIVA for laparoscopic surgery. Although exploratory analyses suggested potential favorable hemodynamic trends, larger multicenter studies are needed to evaluate comparative safety and clinical relevance.

OtherAbstract.AbstractText: Propofol is a common anesthetic for total intravenous anesthesia (TIVA) in children, but it is associated with injection pain, hemodynamic instability, and respiratory depression during induction. Ciprofol is a newer anesthetic drug. We wanted to find out if ciprofol works as well as propofol for children in laparoscopic surgery.

AbstractText.Label: WHAT DID WE DO AND FIND?

OtherAbstract.AbstractText: We randomly assigned 86 children aged 2 to 12 years to receive either ciprofol or propofol. We found that children who received ciprofol met our predefined criteria to be considered “not worse than” propofol in terms of how quickly the breathing tube could be removed. Both groups recovered similarly, felt similar amounts of pain, and had similar rates of confusion when waking up. Neither group experienced nausea or vomiting after surgery, and serious side effects were rare in both groups.

For children having short laparoscopic surgery, ciprofol performed as well as propofol regarding how quickly the breathing tube could be removed. However, because this was a small, single-center study, larger studies in more hospitals are still needed to confirm these results and check safety in different groups of children.

Article.ArticleTitle: Atorvastatin for the Prevention of Cisplatin-Induced Ototoxicity: A Randomized Controlled Trial.

Abstract.AbstractText: Cisplatin is used to treat a variety of tumors, it has a significant ototoxic effect; as studies show that about 40% to 70% of patients treated with cisplatin suffer hearing loss to some extent, which may lead to social isolation, anxiety, depression, and an overall negative effect on quality of life. Atorvastatin has a promising otoprotective potential based on preclinical and observational evidence, but the clinical evidence remains limited and not definitive. This is a randomized controlled trial aimed to investigate the efficacy of Atorvastatin co-administered during cisplatin chemotherapy against its ototoxicity in patients with solid tumors.

This randomized controlled trial was conducted at the oncology center and the audio-vestibular unit, Minia university, Egypt, involving 56 patients with different solid tumors scheduled to receive cisplatin. Patients were randomized to receive either Atorvastatin 10 mg daily or no intervention. Baseline and final audiograms were obtained, the primary outcome is to measure change in pure-tone audiometric thresholds from baseline to post-treatment in both groups. The secondary outcome is to assess severity (grade) of hearing loss as well as the subjective hearing impairment in both groups using the National Cancer Institute-Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events (NCI-CTCAE) V.6 and the Speech, Spatial, and Qualities of Hearing Scale (SSQ) short version (SSQ12) questionnaire, respectively.

A percentage of 41.38% of the case group and 44.4% of the control group experienced cisplatin-induced ototoxicity (CIO) according to NCI-CTCAE V.6 criteria. No significant difference was found between cases and controls regarding CIO measured by audiogram or data obtained from patients through the SSQ12 questionnaire.
Use of atorvastatin (10 mg daily) was not significantly associated with a reduction in CIO, as assessed by change in hearing thresholds, CTCAE criteria, or SSQ12 questionnaire.

OtherAbstract.AbstractText: :Ototoxicity is a common adverse effect of cisplatin chemotherapy. Multiple studies investigated protective agents against CIO, and atorvastatin seems to have a potential benefit based on retrospective data.
:We examined whether co-treatment with atorvastatin during cisplatin chemotherapy can protect against CIO.

:Patients were randomly assigned to case group (received atorvastatin 10 mg daily during cisplatin chemotherapy), and control group (no intervention). Patients received audiometric evaluations before and after treatment to assess the change in hearing status and whether there is a significant difference between the two groups. CTCAE V.6 criteria were used to grade hearing loss, and SSQ12 questionnaire was used at the end of treatment to assess hearing in everyday situations.
:Cisplatin showed significant ototoxicity. Treatment with atorvastatin at a dose of 10 mg daily was not associated with a statistically significant protective effect against CIO in the present study.

Article.ArticleTitle: The Relationship Between Pre-Operative Ipilimumab and Nivolumab Pharmacokinetics and Treatment Outcome in Locoregionally Advanced Urothelial Cancer.

Abstract.AbstractText: Patients with locoregionally advanced urothelial cancer (UC) received three pre-operative cycles of ipilimumab and nivolumab in the NABUCCO trial, across three cohorts with different dosing combinations. This study aimed to define the pharmacokinetics (PK) of both drugs in this population and to assess the relationship between the PK and treatment response. Ipilimumab and nivolumab serum concentrations were measured in 139 samples of 52 patients. A population PK model was developed for both drugs using nonlinear mixed-effects modeling. This model was used to examine baseline clearance (CL0)- and exposure-response relationships, with pathological response at surgery as efficacy parameter. A logistic regression model was constructed to quantify these relationships. The developed population PK model adequately described ipilimumab and nivolumab observations. Individual CL0 estimates of both drugs were correlated (correlation coefficient = 0.57). Among patients in the lowest quartile of CL0 of both drugs, twelve out of thirteen patients were responders. In the logistic regression model, a relatively low nivolumab CL0 and high ipilimumab exposure were successfully related to treatment response. The model predicted probability of response was higher for high-dose ipilimumab (3 mg/kg) compared to low-dose ipilimumab (1 mg/kg) (54% vs. 29%, respectively), and was in line with NABUCCO trial outcomes. These results support the hypothesis that for ipilimumab, an exposure-response relationship exists, while this is not the case for nivolumab. Further confirmation of these relationships is warranted, given the limited number of patients included in the analysis.

OtherAbstract.AbstractText: What is the current knowledge on the topic? ○. In the NABUCCO trial, three cycles of pre‐operative ipilimumab and nivolumab were administered to patients with locoregionally advanced urothelial cancer (UC). In three cohorts, different dosing combinations were administered, leading to substantially different treatment outcomes. In patients with UC, the pharmacokinetics (PK) of ipilimumab and nivolumab have not yet been defined and/or related to treatment outcome. What question did this study address? ○. This study aimed to define the PK of pre‐operative ipilimumab and nivolumab in patients with locoregionally advanced UC and, subsequently, relate it to treatment outcome. Therefore, a population PK model was constructed and, subsequently, individual PK estimates were related to treatment response using logistic regression. What does this study add to our knowledge? ○. Individual baseline clearance (CL0) estimates of ipilimumab and nivolumab were correlated. Patients with the lowest CL0 of both drugs were nearly all treatment responders. A combination of a relatively low nivolumab CL0 and high ipilimumab exposure was related to better treatment response. The findings support the hypothesis that for ipilimumab an exposure–response relationship exists, while this is not the case for nivolumab. However, these relationships should be confirmed in further studies, as our findings are based on a limited patient number. How might this change clinical pharmacology or translational science? ○. If the suggested relationships are further confirmed, it should be prioritized to give a relatively high ipilimumab dose (e.g., 3 mg/kg Q3W) in ipilimumab‐nivolumab treatment regimens in locoregionally advanced UC, to maximize the probability of response. In the future, a predicted probability of response, calculated based on an individual's PK estimates, could be a part of treatment decision making.

Article.ArticleTitle: The Effect of Adding a Home-Based Exercise Programme to Corticosteroid Injection for Plantar Fasciitis on Pain and Functional Performance: A Single-Centre, Randomised Clinical Study.

Abstract.AbstractText: Plantar fasciitis is a common cause of heel pain and functional impairment. Combining injections with exercise may improve treatment outcomes, but evidence of its additional benefit is limited.

In a single-centre, randomised clinical study, adults aged 18 and older with plantar fasciitis were randomised into two groups: Group I (corticosteroid injection only) and Group II (corticosteroid injection + exercise programme). Both groups received a corticosteroid injection. Participants in Group II followed a home-based exercise programme performed 3 days a week for 6 weeks. This programme consisted of exercises to strengthen the intrinsic foot muscles with 3 kg resistance, stretching exercises for the plantar fascia, gastrocnemius muscle, and Achilles tendon, as well as cold massage applications directed at the foot arch. Primary outcome measures were the Visual Analog Scale (VAS), the 6-min walk test (6MWT), and the 50-m walk test (50MWT); Secondary outcome measures were shortness tests, American Orthopaedic Foot and Ankle Society (AOFAS) midfoot and hindfoot scores, and the Foot Function Index (FFI). Assessments were performed at baseline, week 3, and week 6. At the week 3 assessment, 40 participants were evaluated (18 in Group I and 22 in Group II). By week 6, 24 participants (11 in Group I and 13 in Group II) had completed the follow-up assessment and were included in the final analysis.

At baseline, there were differences between the groups regarding various AOFAS subscales and the FFI. However, these differences were no longer present at the follow-up assessments, and no significant intergroup difference was detected at either follow-up time point. In both groups, primary outcomes (VAS, 6MWT, and 50MWT) and most secondary outcomes showed significant improvements at weeks 3 and 6 compared to baseline values. No significant changes were observed in AOFAS alignment scores, with the exception of hindfoot alignment in Group II at week 6.

Although no significant difference was found between the groups, improvements in pain and function were maintained in both groups throughout the 6-week follow-up period. In patients with plantar fasciitis, both corticosteroid injection alone and corticosteroid injection combined with a home exercise programme were associated with short-term improvements in pain and functional outcomes.
ClinicalTrials.gov NCT06917937 (retrospectively registered) LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level II, Therapeutic and prospective randomised trial.

Article.ArticleTitle: Effects of Omega-3 Supplementation on Inflammatory Biomarkers and Ambulatory and Central Blood Pressure in Patients Treated for Hypertension and Dyslipidemia: A Randomized, Double-Blind, Placebo-Controlled Trial.

Abstract.AbstractText: Omega-3 fatty acids exert anti-inflammatory and hemodynamic effects; however, their concurrent effects in patients receiving treatment for hypertension and dyslipidemia remain incompletely characterized.

To evaluate the effects of 12 weeks of supplementation with pharmaceutical-grade omega-3 fatty acids on inflammatory biomarkers, central and brachial blood pressure including office and 24 h ambulatory measurements, and vascular function in this population.

In this exploratory, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled pilot trial, 100 adults received omega-3 ethyl esters at a capsule dose of 2 g/day or a matching placebo for 12 weeks, in addition to stable usual pharmacological treatment. Treatment effects were estimated using linear mixed-effects models. p-values were nominal, and 95% confidence intervals were not adjusted for multiplicity.

Compared with placebo, omega-3 supplementation was associated with greater reductions in the neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio (NLR; -0.43; 95% CI, -0.73 to -0.13; p = 0.005), ferritin (-47.32 ng/mL; 95% CI, -77.55 to -17.08; p = 0.003), daytime systolic blood pressure (-6.52 mmHg; 95% CI, -10.66 to -2.39; p = 0.002), nighttime diastolic blood pressure (-5.55 mmHg; 95% CI, -9.87 to -1.22; p = 0.013), central systolic blood pressure (-6.71 mmHg; 95% CI, -12.22 to -1.20; p = 0.019), and estimated pulse wave velocity (-0.77 m/s; 95% CI, -1.19 to -0.36; p < 0.001).

The trial identified exploratory signals involving NLR, ferritin, selected ambulatory blood-pressure measures, central systolic blood pressure, and algorithm-derived ePWV. Multiplicity, limited sample size, and incomplete outcome availability preclude confirmatory interpretation. Independent replication in larger, prospectively registered trials with clearly specified endpoints and reproducible sample-size calculations is required.

Article.ArticleTitle: Vitamin D and Particulate Matter-Associated Immune Responses in People Living with HIV: A Randomized Trial with Exploratory DNA Methylation Analyses.

Abstract.AbstractText: HIV-infected individuals with compromised immune function are particularly vulnerable to atmospheric particulate matter (PM). While Vitamin D is known to modulate inflammation and immune function, its effect on PM-induced immune impairment in HIV-infected individuals remains unclear.

This randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial in Wuhan, China, investigated Vitamin D's protective effects. In total, 80 participants received daily Vitamin D or a placebo and were followed up every 28 days across four visits. PM exposure was assessed 72 h before each follow-up, with immune cell counts, immunomodulatory factors, and whole-genome DNA methylation profiles measured. Linear mixed-effects models were used to assess the association between PM exposure and cell counts, and to identify CpG sites associated with Vitamin D. Mediating models further evaluated the role of these CpG sites in linking Vitamin D intervention to cytokine changes.

From March to July, 2023, 75 participants received 271 follow-ups. Vitamin D supplementation significantly attenuated the negative associations between PM exposure and CD4+T cell and CD19+B cell counts. Compared with the placebo group, the estimated PM-associated changes in CD4+T cell counts differed by 3.37%, 2.21%, and 1.96% per 10 µg/m3 increase in PM1, PM2.5, and PM10 concentrations, respectively, while the corresponding differences for CD19+B cell counts were 4.71%, 2.98%, and 2.65%, respectively. Significant methylation changes were observed at 173 CpG sites related to Vitamin D. Of these, 25 sites-including cg27066321 (PEX14), cg08500112 (PDE4D), and cg25882580 (CACNG6)-were identified as potential mediators of the effects of vitamin D supplementation on TLR4, IL-6, and TNF-α levels, with mediation proportions ranging from 27.98% to 78.78%.
Vitamin D supplementation may attenuate PM-associated immune alterations in people living with HIV, with DNA methylation potentially contributing to the underlying mechanisms.

Article.ArticleTitle: Feasibility of Implementing a Dietary Intervention in Older Adults with Mild Depressive Symptoms and Low Activity: Lessons Learned.

Abstract.AbstractText: Background/Objectives: Several dietary interventions of blueberry intake have been performed for a wide variety of clinical outcomes (e.g., cardiovascular, bone), but none have been conducted in older adults with mild depressive symptoms and low activity. Such individuals may represent a unique group who may be in particular need of a lifestyle change, but lack the motivation to engage in an intervention. Thus, our goal was to test the feasibility of a dietary intervention in which older adults with mild depressive symptoms and low activity were randomly assigned to consume 48 g of freeze-dried blueberry or placebo powder each day for 3 months. Methods: Individuals were recruited by various methods (e.g., targeted web-based advertisements, flyers, etc.). Our primary assessment of feasibility was retention rate (e.g., the percentage of individuals that completed the intervention out of the total randomized); however, other metrics like recruitment rate, safety, and compliance were also evaluated. We pre-specified that the study would be considered feasible if 80% of the individuals that were randomized to the intervention completed the study. Results: Our study found that 76% (95%CI: 59-93; n = 22 out of 29) of the individuals randomized to the intervention went on to complete the intervention, which is close to, but does not satisfy our pre-specified feasibility threshold. Among individuals that completed the study, compliance with the study powder over the 3 months was relatively high (≥87% in both groups). There were no serious adverse events, and only 10 adverse events that occurred similarly across groups (n = 6 in placebo, n = 4 in blueberry). Conclusions: Together, our data provides evidence that a dietary intervention supplementing a relatively high dose of blueberry powder in a unique population of older adults is possible and adherence was high among those that completed the intervention.

Article.ArticleTitle: Effects of Whole "Navelina" Orange Consumption on Glucose Homeostasis and Fructosamine Levels in Patients with Metabolic Dysfunction-Associated Steatotic Liver Disease (MASLD): A Randomized Controlled Trial.

Abstract.AbstractText: Background: Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) is closely linked to insulin resistance and altered glucose and lipid metabolism. Fructosamine assays can provide complementary information regarding short-term glycemic exposure, making them particularly useful in the context of short-term nutritional interventions. This study evaluated the effects of whole "Navelina" orange consumption on glucose homeostasis in patients with MASLD. Methods: Sixty patients with MASLD were randomly assigned to an experimental or control arm. The experimental arm consumed 400 g/day of whole "Navelina" oranges for 4 weeks, while controls abstained from orange consumption. Fasting glucose, insulin, fructosamine, HOMA-IR, and QUICKI were assessed at baseline and follow-up. Generalized estimating equation models evaluated time-by-treatment interactions. Exploratory Spearman correlations assessed associations between changes in the lipid and glucose-related parameters. Results: Significant time-treatment interactions were observed for dietary sugars, vitamin A, and vitamin C. No significant interactions were observed for fasting glucose, insulin, HOMA-IR, or QUICKI. Fructosamine levels showed a non-significant trend toward a reduction (p = 0.078). In the experimental arm, changes in LDL levels were positively correlated with HOMA-IR and insulin levels, and inversely correlated with QUICKI. Conclusions: This study is one of the first clinical trials to evaluate the potential impact of whole orange consumption on glucose metabolism. However, these exploratory findings require confirmation through randomized studies conducted on larger samples and over longer periods.

Article.ArticleTitle: Weekly Calcifediol 100 µg in Women with Vitamin D Deficiency: A Post Hoc Analysis of a Randomised Placebo-Controlled Phase II/III Trial.

Abstract.AbstractText: Background/Objective: Given the high prevalence of vitamin D deficiency, particularly among older women, this post hoc analysis was conducted to evaluate the long-term efficacy and safety of weekly calcifediol 100 µg in women with vitamin D deficiency participating in a randomised, double-blind, phase II/III trial. Methods: A total of 261 women were included (calcifediol, n = 192; placebo, n = 69). The primary objective was to compare the proportions of women achieving serum 25(OH)D concentrations ≥20 ng/mL or ≥30 ng/mL over the 12-month treatment period. Exploratory analyses of body mass index (BMI) and menopausal status were performed. Results: Weekly calcifediol 100 µg demonstrated superior efficacy versus placebo from week 4 in women achieving ≥20 ng/mL (68.2% vs. 5.8%; p < 0.001) or ≥30 ng/mL (21.4% vs. 0%; p < 0.001), and consistently higher proportions were maintained through week 52. Mean 25(OH)D concentrations increased from 12.21 ng/mL at baseline to 39.47 ng/mL at week 16, and remained stable (41-43 ng/mL) thereafter. No significant differences were observed across BMI or menopausal status subgroups. The safety profile of weekly calcifediol 100 µg was similar to placebo, with no evidence of toxicity. Conclusions: Weekly calcifediol 100 µg is a safe and effective option for achieving and maintaining adequate vitamin D levels in vitamin D-deficient women over a period of 12 months, and is associated with consistent effects across BMI and menopausal status.

Article.ArticleTitle: Effect of Timing of Apple Juice Consumption on Postprandial Glycemia: A Randomized Crossover Trial.

Abstract.AbstractText: Background/Objectives: Fruit juice is commonly consumed with meals, yet its liquid matrix and rapidly absorbable carbohydrates may influence postprandial glycemic excursions. Whether altering the timing of fruit juice intake relative to a meal can attenuate postprandial glucose (PPG) remains unclear. This study aimed to investigate the effect of the timing of apple juice consumption on PPG in healthy adults. Methods: This randomized, two-period crossover trial (ChiCTR2600121025) enrolled 20 healthy adults in Beijing, China (March 2026), randomized 1:1; 19 with valid continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) data were analyzed. Each consumed 200 mL of 100% apple juice either 30 min before a standardized breakfast (preload) or with the same breakfast (co-ingestion), separated by a 4-day washout. Standardized lunch and dinner were provided. Blinding was not feasible. The primary outcome was breakfast peak glucose measured by CGM; secondary outcomes were incremental area under the curve (iAUC0-210), maximum excursion, and the corresponding lunch and dinner outcomes. Results: Preloading significantly reduced breakfast peak glucose versus co-ingestion (mean difference 0.51 mmol/L; 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.07-0.94; p = 0.025) and breakfast maximum glucose excursion (0.42 mmol/L; 95% CI 0.02-0.82; p = 0.040), but not iAUC0-210 (0.07 mmol/L·h; 95% CI -0.57 to 0.70; p = 0.830); no glycemic outcome differed at lunch or dinner. Conclusions: Consuming the same serving of apple juice 30 min before breakfast, rather than with it, reduced breakfast peak glucose and maximum glucose excursion. For individuals who already consume fruit juice, adjusting its timing relative to breakfast reduced breakfast peak glucose and maximum glucose excursion in this small sample; confirmation in larger trials is needed.

Article.ArticleTitle: Effect of a 3-Month Modified, High-Quality Take-Home Ration on Linear Growth and Body Composition in Rural South Indian Infants Aged 6-9 Months: A Cluster-Randomized Controlled Trial.

Abstract.AbstractText: Background/Objectives: Linear growth faltering remains a major public health concern in low- and middle-income countries, wherein sub-optimal complementary feeding and hygiene practices are key modifiable factors. Inadequate complementary feeding is addressed through government-issued Take-Home Ration (THR) for <3-year-old children. This THR is not consumed regularly and does not bridge deficits in protein quality and fat intake among South Indian rural children. The addition of milk and legumes into a reformulated THR would address these gaps, but its efficacy remains unknown. Methods: In this 3-month cluster-randomized controlled trial among rural infants (6-9 months old), the intervention group (12 village clusters; n = 67) received a modified milk-and legume-based THR along with standard government THR, while the control group (12 village clusters; n = 67) received standard government THR alone. Caregivers of both groups were educated on nutrition and hygiene practices. Anthropometry, body composition (BC), morbidity, diet, and compliance data were collected. The primary outcome (length-for-age z-score (LAZ)) and secondary outcomes were analyzed using cluster-adjusted linear mixed models (LMM) in an intention-to-treat analysis. Results: While LAZ did not differ significantly between groups (β = 0.063 LAZ/month, 95%CI: -0.019, 0.145; p = 0.130), adjusted LMM showed significant differences in length (0.213 cm/month, 95%CI: 0.025, 0.400, p = 0.027), weight (0.040 kg/month, 95%CI: 0.001, 0.079, p = 0.044) and head circumference (0.067 cm/month, 95%CI: 0.005, 0.128, p = 0.033). LAZ decreased in both groups, with a significantly lower decline in the intervention group (slope difference: β = 0.05, 95% CI: 0.006, 0.095, p = 0.027). BC did not differ significantly. Conclusions: Improving protein quality and fat content of the government-issued THR showed a favourable LAZ trajectory among infants from rural South India. (Clinical Trial Registry-India: CTRI/2020/06/025825).

Article.ArticleTitle: Effects of Heat-Killed Lactiplantibacillus plantarum L-137 on Menopause-Related Outcomes and Gut Barrier-Related Biomarkers in Japanese Women: A Randomized, Double-Blind, Placebo-Controlled Trial.

Abstract.AbstractText: Background/Objectives: Menopause-related issues-such as mood disturbance, hot flashes, and sleep disturbance-are thought to be influenced not only by hormonal changes but also by everyday stress and gut barrier-related host responses. Heat-killed Lactiplantibacillus plantarum L-137 (HK L-137) has shown immunomodulatory and gut barrier-related effects, but clinical evidence for its effects in menopausal women is limited. We investigated whether HK L-137 intake affects menopause-related outcomes and gut barrier-related biomarkers in women reporting daily stress. Methods: We conducted a 12-week randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, parallel-group trial in healthy Japanese women aged 45-69 years who self-reported daily stress (UMIN000055687). Participants were randomly assigned to receive one tablet containing 10 mg HK L-137 or placebo daily. Mood state, menopausal symptoms, and sleep quality-as menopause-related outcomes-and gut barrier-related biomarkers were assessed at baseline and week 12. Results: A total of 121 participants were included, and 119 completed the study. No significant between-group differences were observed in the questionnaire scores of mood state, menopausal symptoms, or sleep quality. Changes in serum soluble CD14 (sCD14) and lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) differed significantly between groups, favoring the HK L-137 group (p = 0.020 and p = 0.010, respectively). In the prespecified subgroup with higher baseline levels of negative mood, HK L-137 significantly improved hot flashes item and sleep maintenance score, and was associated with favorable changes in sCD14, LDH, and body mass index versus placebo. No intervention-related safety concerns were identified. Conclusions: HK L-137 favorably affected sCD14 and LDH in the overall analysis and improved selected menopause-related outcomes in women with higher baseline levels of negative mood. These findings suggest a possible role of gut barrier-related host responses associated with microbial translocation.

Article.ArticleTitle: Fruit Smoothie Supplementation and Inflammatory Biomarkers in Individuals Receiving Opioid Agonist Therapy: A Multicenter Randomized Controlled Trial.

Abstract.AbstractText: Background/Objectives: People with opioid dependence often experience elevated inflammatory markers and poor dietary habits. Evidence from other populations suggests that higher fruit and vegetable intake may reduce inflammation. This multicenter randomized controlled trial investigates whether offering a daily supplementation of 250 mL of fruit smoothie for 16 weeks to people undergoing opioid agonist treatment (OAT) can reduce inflammation biomarkers. Methods: 319 individuals were randomized to receive either a daily supplement of 250 mL of fruit smoothie in addition to standard OAT or standard OAT alone over 16 weeks. The primary outcome was the log-transformed change in high-sensitivity C-reactive protein (hs-CRP). Secondary outcomes included changes in cytokines (IL-8, IL-1RA, and MCP-1) and leukocyte counts. Results: No between-group differences were observed in changes in hs-CRP levels (0.96 (0.77; 1.21) mg/L), leukocytes (0.99 (0.93; 1.05)109/L), IL-8 (1.10 (0.84; 1.46) pg/mL), MCP-1 (0.94 (0.80; 1.11) pg/mL), and IL-1RA (1.06 (0.91; 1.23) pg/mL). High levels of inflammatory markers were observed at baseline in both the intervention group and the control group. Conclusions: After 16 weeks of offering fruit smoothie supplementation in patients receiving OAT, we did not detect a between-group reduction in inflammation markers such as hs-CRP, IL-8, MCP-1, IL-1RA, and leukocyte counts, under the achieved level of delivery and exposure. Nonetheless, persistently high levels of inflammatory markers were observed in this study.

Article.ArticleTitle: The Preliminary Effects of Capsaicin Supplementation on Cerebrovascular Function and Cognition in Middle-Aged and Older Adults Who Are Overweight or Obese.

Abstract.AbstractText: Background/Objectives: Cerebrovascular function and cognition decline with age and may be further exacerbated by obesity. Capsaicin may improve cerebrovascular function and cognition, although evidence in humans is lacking. We investigated the effects of 12 weeks of capsaicin supplementation on cerebrovascular function and cognition in middle-aged and older adults who were overweight or obese. Methods: Forty participants were randomly allocated to receive 200 mg/day of Capsifen® or a placebo, with 34 completing the intervention (n = 17 in both). Before and after supplementation, transcranial Doppler ultrasonography was used to measure the cerebrovascular responsiveness (CVR) to physiological (hypercapnia, 5% carbon dioxide) and cognitive stimuli, while cognition was assessed using a comprehensive cognitive battery. The trial was prospectively registered (ACTRN12623000556640). Results: Total CVR to cognitive stimuli increased following Capsifen® supplementation (18 ± 3% to 21 ± 1%) and decreased in the placebo group (21 ± 4% to 19 ± 3%; p = 0.0002). Total cognition increased following Capsifen® supplementation (98 ± 18 to 107 ± 18) compared with the placebo (105 ± 13 to 106 ± 10; p = 0.0085). Capsifen® did not alter CVR to hypercapnia (30 ± 18% to 44 ± 27% vs. 39 ± 23% to 32 ± 16%; p = 0.5981). Working memory, executive function and exercise performance also improved, while waist circumference and waist-to-hip ratio decreased. Conclusions: Twelve weeks of Capsifen® supplementation improved total cognition and CVR to cognitive stimuli but not CVR to hypercapnia. These findings provide preliminary evidence that chronic capsaicin supplementation may improve cognition and neurovascular coupling in humans.

Article.ArticleTitle: Targeted Colostrum Bioactive Proteins Improve Gastrointestinal Symptoms and Modulate the Gut Microbiome: A Randomised Double-Blind Placebo-Controlled Trial.

Abstract.AbstractText: Gastrointestinal (GI) symptoms such as indigestion, bloating and reflux are common and can negatively affect quality of life. Bovine colostrum is a rich source of nutrients and other bioactive constituents that has been shown to be beneficial for gut health.

This 12-week, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, 3-arm study aimed to evaluate the effects of MaolactinGI™, a proprietary bovine colostrum supplement, on upper GI symptoms and gut microbiome composition in healthy adults aged 18 years and older experiencing moderate GI discomfort. Participants completed a 4-week run-in period followed by an 8-week intervention period. Outcomes measured included changes in upper GI symptoms via the Gastrointestinal Symptom Rating Scale (GSRS), Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease Questionnaire (GerdQ), Bloating Symptoms Visual Analogue Scale (BSVAS), Digestion-associated Quality of Life Questionnaire (DQLQ), Bristol Stool Chart, intestinal permeability, faecal calprotectin, serum inflammatory markers, gut microbiome analyses, blood safety markers and adverse events.

Ninety eligible participants were allocated to either the high-dose (500 mg/day), low-dose (250 mg/day), or placebo groups, and data from 83 participants were analysed. The high-dose MaolactinGI™ group demonstrated statistically significant improvements in the total GSRS score and DQLQ score compared with placebo, suggesting a meaningful reduction in total symptom burden and improved quality of life. The improvements in GSRS were clinically meaningful in size, supporting the practical relevance of MaolactinGI™ for adults experiencing everyday upper GI discomfort. High-dose supplementation also preserved microbial richness relative to placebo (Chao1); exploratory within-group analyses further indicated enrichment of SCFA-associated commensal taxa. The intervention was well tolerated and demonstrated an acceptable safety profile.
These findings support the potential of targeted colostrum-derived bioactive protein fractions as a novel nutritional strategy for supporting GI health and microbiome balance.

Article.ArticleTitle: Time-Restricted Eating as a Dietary Intervention for Polyendocrine Metabolic Ovarian Syndrome (PMOS): Protocol for a Randomized Controlled Trial.

Abstract.AbstractText: Time-restricted eating (TRE) appears to be a promising dietary strategy for women with polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome (PMOS), with potential benefits for insulin resistance and metabolic health. Emerging evidence also suggests that TRE may be associated with changes in gut microbiota composition and microbial metabolites, as well as circulating biomarkers involved in metabolic regulation. However, the relationships among these factors remain poorly understood.

The aim of this study is to test the hypothesis that adding TRE to Healthy Eating Plate recommendations is more effective in improving insulin resistance, assessed using HOMA-IR, than Healthy Eating Plate recommendations alone in women with PMOS. Exploratory analyses will investigate changes in gut microbiota composition, microbial metabolites, and circulating concentrations of neuroactive compounds.

This two-arm, parallel-group randomized controlled trial will compare 8-h TRE with unrestricted meal timing in women aged 18 to 40 years with PMOS and a BMI of 25-40 kg/m2 with a 1:1 allocation ratio. Both groups will receive Healthy Eating Plate-based dietary advice and attend four visits; the TRE protocol will be followed for 8 weeks. The primary outcome will be a change in HOMA-IR from baseline to week 8. We will also assess changes in glucose and lipid metabolism, circulating neuroactive compounds, including GABA and kisspeptin, anthropometric parameters, hormonal profile, composition and diversity of the microbiota and its metabolites.

We anticipate that this study will expand the limited evidence regarding TRE in women with PMOS and provide exploratory insights into the relationships among gut microbiota composition, microbial metabolites, circulating GABA and kisspeptin, and insulin resistance. The findings may help identify potential mechanisms underlying the metabolic effects of TRE in this population.
1.1, August 2026.
Participant recruitment has not yet commenced.

Article.ArticleTitle: Examining the Gastrointestinal Effects of Solnul®, a Prebiotic Resistant Potato Starch: A Replication Randomized, Double-Blind, Placebo-Controlled Clinical Trial in Healthy Adults.

Abstract.AbstractText: A prebiotic is a substrate that is selectively utilized by host microbiota to confer a health benefit. Consumption of 3.5 g of Solnul® resistant potato starch (RPS) was previously shown to selectively increase Bifidobacterium and Akkermansia, as well as improve stool form relative to a placebo. The objective of this study was to reproduce these effects in an independent cohort.

A 4-week, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, parallel group trial evaluated the effects of 3.5 g RPS versus a placebo on changes in Bifidobacterium, Akkermansia, stool form, and bowel movement (BM) frequency using 16s rRNA sequencing, the Bristol Stool Form Scale, and personal diaries in healthy adults aged 18-69 years in Guelph, ON.

Compared to the placebo (n = 35), the relative abundance of Bifidobacterium increased (p = 0.049, Brunner-Munzel), and the number of normal stools (Type 3 or 4) was higher in the RPS group (n = 35; p = 0.0077, Chi-Square; key secondary endpoints). While differences were not observed for Akkermansia relative to the placebo (p = 0.49; primary endpoint), End-of-Study Akkermansia levels were higher than Run-In levels for RPS (p = 0.046, Wilcoxon signed-rank) but not the placebo (p = 0.14). Participants consuming RPS had higher BM frequency at the End-of-Study compared to the Run-In period, but the effect was not different from the placebo. Comparing End-of-Study and Run-In periods, the RPS group experienced fewer days without a BM relative to the placebo. No changes in the GSRS or serious adverse events were reported in the RPS group.
This clinical trial confirmed that 3.5 g of RPS induces a bifidogenic effect and normalized stool form, consistent with the previous study. NCT06949631.

Article.ArticleTitle: Probiotic-Enriched Yogurt with Encapsulated Lacticaseibacillus rhamnosus and Bacillus clausii: Product Characterization and Quality of Life Assessment in Type 2 Diabetes.

Abstract.AbstractText: Probiotic-enriched foods represent a promising nutritional approach for supporting health in chronic metabolic diseases. Yogurt provides a suitable food matrix for probiotic incorporation, while microencapsulation may improve probiotic stability during storage and consumption.

The aim of this study was to develop and characterize a yogurt containing encapsulated Lacticaseibacillus rhamnosus (L. rhamnosus) and Bacillus clausii (B. clausii) and to evaluate its effects on selected dimensions of health-related quality of life (HRQoL) in patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM). A probiotic-enriched yogurt was prepared using alginate-starch capsules containing L. rhamnosus and B. clausii. The product was evaluated during three weeks of refrigerated storage for pH, syneresis, water holding capacity, color, and probiotic viability. A randomized, two-arm, placebo-controlled interventional study was conducted in patients with T2DM. Participants received either probiotic yogurt containing encapsulated probiotics or a placebo yogurt containing probiotic-free capsules. HRQoL was assessed at baseline and post-intervention using the RAND 36-Item Health Survey (RAND 36).

During three weeks of refrigerated storage, the yogurt showed a progressive decrease in pH and syneresis, while water holding capacity remained indicative of good structural stability. Only minor changes in color were observed, and culturable microorganisms remained recoverable from the capsules during refrigerated storage. In an exploratory, placebo-controlled pilot evaluation, 54 patients with T2DM received two 100 g servings per week for three weeks. After Holm correction for multiple comparisons, the group × time interaction remained significant for vitality (adjusted p = 0.004) and emotional well-being (adjusted p = 0.009) but not for physical role limitations; in baseline-adjusted ANCOVA (Analysis of Variance), emotional well-being showed the most consistent evidence (adjusted difference 8.3 points, 95% CI 3.5-13.2), whereas results for vitality and physical role limitations were sensitive to model specification.

Baseline HRQoL was substantially higher in the probiotic group, limiting causal interpretation. The yogurt showed favorable technological stability with culturable microorganisms persisting in the capsules during storage; the preliminary HRQoL signal requires confirmation in an adequately powered trial.

Article.ArticleTitle: Effects of a Nutrigenetic Diet on Fat Mass Loss, Insulin Resistance, and Subclinical Inflammation in Adults with Abdominal Obesity: A Randomized Controlled Trial-The INNUPREC Study.

Abstract.AbstractText: Background: Abdominal obesity (AO) is involved in the development of cardiometabolic disorders, in which factors such as diet and genetics play crucial roles. In this context, interactions between genetic variants and dietary responses may influence metabolic processes associated with AO. Objective: This study aimed to evaluate the effects of a nutrigenetic diet incorporating 21 genetic variants related to lipid metabolism and cardiovascular risk on anthropometric and biochemical parameters and antioxidant capacity in adults with AO. Methods: An eight-week randomized controlled trial was conducted in 58 adults with AO, who were randomly assigned to either a nutrigenetics-guided diet or a standard diet. Participants in the nutrigenetic group underwent genotyping for 21 variants associated with lipid metabolism and cardiometabolic risk in the ABCA1, APOA1, APOA2, APOA5, APOB, APOC3, APOE, CETP, CDKN2B-AS1, CD36, FABP2, FTO, LIPC, LPL, MTTP, MTHFR, NFKB1, PON1, SIRT1, and ZPR1 genes. Anthropometric and biochemical measurements were performed. Antioxidant and oxidative stress biomarkers were measured using colorimetric assays and ELISA, respectively. Results: In baseline-adjusted ANCOVA models controlling for age and sex, with false discovery rate (FDR) correction, both groups achieved comparable reductions in body weight and fat mass under equivalent energy restriction. However, the nutrigenetic group demonstrated significantly greater improvements in insulin levels, HOMA-IR, and high-sensitivity C-reactive protein (hs-CRP) compared with the standard diet group. The nutrigenetic intervention also resulted in greater reductions in the prevalence of elevated TyG index (-20% vs. -10.8%) and HOMA-IR (-33.3% vs. -10.7%), along with a trend toward a greater increase in catalase activity. Conclusions: Compared with a standard dietary intervention, a nutrigenetic diet was associated with greater improvements in fasting insulin, estimated insulin resistance (HOMA-IR), and systemic inflammation (hs-CRP) in adults with AO.

Article.ArticleTitle: Comparative Effects of Different Carbohydrate-Protein Formulations on Resistance Training Adaptations in Healthy Young Men.

Abstract.AbstractText: Background/Objectives: Evidence is limited on whether carbohydrate formulations enhance resistance training adaptations when protein intake is relatively adequate. This study compared two carbohydrate-protein formulations in healthy young men. Methods: In this randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, 36 untrained men aged 18-25 years were assigned to a maltodextrin-based carbohydrate control group (PLA), low-molecular-weight carbohydrate plus protein (LMW-CHO+PRO), or high-molecular-weight carbohydrate plus protein (HMW-CHO+PRO). Thirty-three participants completed 8 weeks of supervised resistance training three times weekly and daily supplementation (50 g). Body composition, muscle circumference and thickness, strength, and serum testosterone, cortisol, and testosterone-to-cortisol ratio were assessed before and after intervention. The trial was registered with the Chinese Clinical Trial Registry (ChiCTR2500110509). Results: Body mass, total muscle mass, muscle circumference and thickness, and strength improved in all groups. Both supplementation groups showed greater improvements than PLA across several muscular adaptation measures. Time × group interactions were significant for body mass and total muscle mass, but not fat mass. HMW-CHO+PRO produced greater increases in body mass and total muscle mass than LMW-CHO+PRO; however, no consistent differences between formulations were observed in regional muscle circumference, muscle thickness, strength, or blood biomarkers. Conclusions: Under conditions of relatively adequate protein intake, combined carbohydrate and protein supplementation may provide additional support for resistance training adaptations. These findings do not establish an overall advantage of either formulation, nor can the observed differences be attributed specifically to carbohydrate molecular weight.

Article.ArticleTitle: Boosting Post-Stroke Recovery: The Role of Nutritional Supplementation in Reducing Fatigue-A Single-Blind Randomized Controlled Trial.

Abstract.AbstractText: Post-stroke fatigue (PSF) remains a debilitating barrier to recovery. Chronic inflammation and oxidative stress often create physiological plateaus that standard rehabilitation alone cannot resolve. This single-blind randomized controlled trial (RCT) evaluated the efficacy of Food for Special Medical Purposes formulated with iron and other vitamins and minerals in Sucrosomial® form, allowing improved absorption, bioavailability, and tolerability, as an adjunct to neurorehabilitation. One hundred and twenty stroke patients were randomized into an experimental group (Sid-G) receiving the specific nutraceutical compound or a control group (CG) receiving standard care. Longitudinal assessments from baseline (T0) through 16 weeks (T3) measured clinical outcomes (including fatigue, motor/cognitive function) and physiological markers, specifically phase angle (PhA) derived from Bioimpedance Analysis, and key inflammatory and oxidative stress biomarkers (IL-6 and MPO). The Sid-G cohort demonstrated superior, sustained improvements in fatigue, motor, and cognitive function (p < 0.05). These clinical gains were reflected in the following physiological observations: the time × group interaction for cellular integrity (SPhA) was not significant, though within-group improvements were observed in Sid-G (p = 0.009); at the group level, significant time × group interactions were detected for key inflammatory and oxidative stress markers (IL-6, p = 0.001; MPO, p = 0.026). Correlational analysis revealed a significant association between changes in inflammatory markers and clinical recovery outcomes in Sid-G, a pattern absent in the CG. Adjunctive supplementation may support recovery by helping patients to overcome physiological plateaus. These findings support further evaluation of an integrated, metabolically focused approach to neurorehabilitation.

Article.ArticleTitle: Efficacy and Safety of Cuban Policosanol on Cognitive Function and Antioxidant Status in Adults with Subjective Memory Decline: A 12-Week Randomized, Double-Blinded, Placebo-Controlled Multicenter Trial.

Abstract.AbstractText: Objectives: Early non-pharmacological interventions for people with subjective memory decline (SMD) are increasingly advocated in preventing age-related cognitive decline and potentially delaying progression to mild cognitive impairment or dementia. In this multicenter clinical trial (RAYDELP1), we evaluated the efficacy and safety of sugarcane-derived Cuban policosanol (PCO) on cognitive function, superoxide dismutase (SOD) activity, inflammatory markers, and metabolic panels in adults aged 55-85 years with subjective cognitive complaints. Methods: A 12-week, randomized, double-blinded, placebo-controlled trial was conducted at Gachon University Gil Medical Center and Seoul Veterans Hospital in adults with SMD complaints. Individuals were randomized equally into three groups: placebo, PCO 20 mg group, or PCO 40 mg group. Assessment of cognitive function was performed using the Alzheimer's Disease Assessment Scale-Cognitive Subscale (ADAS-Cog 11) and the Korean Mini-Mental State Examination (K-MMSE). All measurements, including SOD activity, inflammatory markers, and metabolic parameters, were analyzed in blood samples at baseline and after 12 weeks. For an exploratory subgroup analysis, participants receiving statins and those with potential ceiling effects or greater cognitive impairment based on K-MMSE scores were excluded. The K-MMSE range of 18-26 was used as an exploratory criterion to reduce heterogeneity in baseline cognitive scores, resulting in a refined analysis population of 56 participants. Results: In the refined SMD population, SOD activity increased significantly in the PCO 40 mg group after 12 weeks (mean change, +0.16 ± 0.25 U/mL; p = 0.0109) with increasing HDL-C, whereas changes in the placebo groups were not statistically significant (+0.08 ± 0.24 U/mL, p = 0.1873) with decreasing HDL-C. HDL-C levels increased in a dose-dependent manner in both the PCO 20 mg (+0.78 ± 5.1 mg/dL) and PCO 40 mg (+2.2 ± 6.7 mg/dL) groups within and between the groups. Both PCO groups showed significant differences compared with placebo in the between-group analysis and baseline-adjusted ANCOVA (p = 0.0124 and p = 0.0142, respectively). K-MMSE place-orientation scores improved significantly from baseline within both PCO groups (20 mg: 0.94 ± 0.87, p = 0.0003; 40 mg: 0.47 ± 0.77, p = 0.0155), whereas no significant within-group change was observed in the placebo group. Similarly, ADAS-Cog 11 language scores improved significantly within both PCO groups (20 mg: -1.17 ± 1.92, p = 0.0194; 40 mg: -0.95 ± 1.58, p = 0.0176). The 20 mg PCO group also showed a significant within-group decrease in Visual CPT false-alarm errors (-3.83 ± 7.13, p = 0.0357). However, between-group comparisons and baseline-adjusted ANCOVA did not demonstrate statistically significant differences in the selected cognitive outcomes. Conclusions: In the analyzed study population, HDL-C levels increased numerically in both PCO groups in a dose-dependent manner. The PCO 40 mg group showed a significant within-group increase in serum SOD activity, while improvements in selected cognitive domains were observed within both 20 mg and 40 mg PCO groups. However, no significant differences were found in between-group or ANCOVA analyses. PCO was well tolerated, and further clinical studies are warranted to confirm these exploratory findings and clarify its potential effects on cognitive function and enhancement of HDL quantity and quality.

Article.ArticleTitle: Efficacy of a Limosilactobacillus reuteri DSM 17938 and BG-R46® Formulation in Predominantly Breastfed Infants with Infant Distress Syndrome: A Randomized Double-Blind Placebo-Controlled Trial.

Abstract.AbstractText: Background: Infant distress syndrome, previously termed Infantile colic, is a common disorder of gut-brain interaction characterized by excessive crying and impaired behavioral regulation. Although Limosilactobacillus reuteri DSM 17938 has shown efficacy in predominantly breastfed infants, treatment responses remain variable, highlighting the need to investigate alternative probiotic formulations. BG-R46™, a strain derived from DSM 17938, exhibits distinct properties in preclinical models, providing a rationale for evaluating the combined formulation. This study investigated the efficacy and tolerability of DSM 17938 plus BG-R46™ compared with placebo in infants with infantile colic. Methods: In this randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, 50 infants were randomized to receive either the probiotic formulation or placebo for 21 days. Forty-eight infants (24 per group) were included in the intention-to-treat and per-protocol analyses. The primary endpoint was the change from baseline to Day 7 in total infant distress time, defined as the sum of awake fussing, crying, and inconsolable crying recorded using the Baby's Day Diary®. Secondary outcomes included crying time, infant behavioral regulation (sleep duration, awake and content behavior, awake fussing, and inconsolable crying), maternal emotional well-being assessed using the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS), and safety. Results: Baseline infant distress time was comparable between groups. At Day 7, infant distress time decreased by 43% in the probiotic group versus 13% in the placebo group (-236.0 ± 111.5 vs. -66.7 ± 100.1 min/day; p < 0.001). At Day 21, reductions reached 62% and 26%, respectively. The probiotic formulation was well tolerated throughout the study. Conclusions: Supplementation with L. reuteri DSM 17938 plus L. reuteri BG-R46™ significantly reduced infant distress compared with placebo.

Article.ArticleTitle: The Effect of Fibre-Rich Gluten Free Products on Glycaemic Regulation, Gut Symptoms, and Targeted Gut Microbial Taxa in Women with Coeliac Disease: A Randomised Controlled Trial.

Abstract.AbstractText: Background: The only treatment for coeliac disease (CeD) is a gluten-free diet. Gluten-containing cereals constitute a major source of dietary fibre, raising concerns about fibre intake for individuals with CeD. Objective: The present study aimed to investigate the effect of pseudocereal-based, fibre-rich gluten-free products on glycaemic regulation in women with CeD. Secondary endpoints were changes in gut symptoms, targeted gut microbial taxa, and inflammatory and metabolic markers. Methods: This double-blind, randomised, controlled trial was conducted remotely and included 30 women with CeD. Participants were allocated to consume either pseudocereal-based, fibre-rich gluten-free products (experimental) or benchmark products (control) for three weeks. Before and after the interventions, participants underwent an oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT), reported gastrointestinal symptoms, and provided blood samples to analyse micronutrients, metabolic markers, and a satiety hormone, and faecal samples for targeted gut microbial taxa analyses. Results: There was no significant difference in the glycaemic response after the intake of fibre-rich products compared with control products. However, a significant reduction in glucose iAUC was observed within the experimental group (p = 0.049). There was no significant change in gut symptoms within or between groups, except for a reduction in diarrhoea in the control group compared with the experimental group. The abundance of five bacterial species was significantly decreased after intake of control products compared to experimental products. Conclusions: Pseudocereal-based, fibre-rich gluten-free products may be included in the diet for women with CeD without affecting gastrointestinal symptoms. Whether these fibre-rich products improve glycaemic regulation and exert effects via alterations in the gut microbiota needs to be further investigated.

Article.ArticleTitle: Effects of Fecal Microbiota Transplantation on Inflammatory Markers in Parkinson's Disease: Exploratory Results from the EFFACE-PD Study.

Abstract.AbstractText: Inflammation and gut dysbiosis are increasingly recognized as important contributors to the pathophysiology of Parkinson's disease (PD). Fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) has emerged as a potential therapeutic strategy aimed at restoring gut microbial balance and modulating inflammatory pathways. The aim of the study was to evaluate the effect of single fecal microbiota transplantation on systemic and gut-related inflammatory biomarkers in patients with PD. This exploratory analysis was conducted as part of the randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled EFFACE-PD study. Fifty-nine participants with PD were randomized to receive either donor-derived FMT or placebo. Serum levels of IL-18 and calprotectin were measured using ELISA before intervention and 3 months after the procedure. Ferritin, leukocyte count, neutrophils, lymphocytes, and neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio (NLR) were assessed at baseline and after twelve months. No statistically significant between-group differences in changes in inflammatory biomarker concentrations were observed. Broader inflammatory markers, including ferritin and leukocyte parameters, also did not differ significantly between groups. We conclude that single FMT did not induce significant changes in systemic inflammatory biomarkers in this exploratory cohort of PD patients. Larger studies with standardized inflammatory assessments are needed to clarify the immunomodulatory effects of FMT in PD.
