Article.ArticleTitle: Low-Level Light Therapy for Dry Eye Disease in Thyroid Eye Disease: A Randomized, Double-Masked, Sham-Controlled Trial.

Abstract.AbstractText: Dry eye disease (DED) affects the majority of patients with thyroid eye disease (TED) and frequently persists despite maximal conservative therapy. Low-level light therapy (LLLT), or photobiomodulation, is a non-invasive treatment with anti-inflammatory and pro-reparative properties whose value in autoimmune, chronically driven ocular surface disease is unknown. In this prospective, randomized, double-masked, sham-controlled trial, eyes of patients with TED-associated DED that remained symptomatic despite intensive preservative-free lubrication, bedtime ophthalmic ointment and daily periocular hygiene were allocated 2:1 to periocular LLLT (630 nm LED mask, 15 min per session, applied over closed eyelids) or to sham treatment (identical procedure with light emission reduced to <30% of therapeutic output). Background ocular surface therapy was maintained unchanged in both arms. Assessments were performed at baseline (T0), weekly during treatment (T1-T3) and at one month (T4) and two months (T5) after the last session. The primary outcome was the Ocular Surface Disease Index (OSDI); secondary outcomes were non-invasive break-up time (NIBUT), fluorescein break-up time (FBUT), Schirmer I test, tear osmolarity, upper- and lower-eyelid meibography, corneal fluorescein staining and lipid-layer grade. The primary OSDI assessment was the change from baseline to T3, the end-of-treatment visit. Additional follow-up assessments were performed at T4 and T5. Forty-six eyes of 46 patients were analyzed (30 LLLT, 16 sham); baseline disease was active in 14/30 (46.7%) and 6/16 (37.5%) eyes, respectively. At T3, adjusted OSDI was lower with LLLT than with sham (between-group difference -7.49 points; 95% CI -11.66 to -3.32; p < 0.001). The difference persisted at T4 and T5 (-11.97 and -16.86 points, respectively; both Holm-adjusted p < 0.001). Tear osmolarity was lower with LLLT at T4 (-10.91 mOsm/L; 95% CI -18.96 to -2.87; p = 0.009) and T5 (-13.81 mOsm/L; 95% CI -22.55 to -5.06; p = 0.004). No multiplicity-adjusted between-group differences were demonstrated for NIBUT, FBUT, Schirmer I test or meibography. The adjusted probability of corneal staining was numerically lower with LLLT (T4: 15.7% vs. 34.7%; risk difference -19.0 percentage points; p = 0.100). In exploratory analyses, the treatment-by-visit-by-activity interaction was significant (p = 0.0159), with OSDI differences of -21.45 and -25.90 points in active disease versus -5.50 and -10.09 points in inactive disease at T4 and T5. CAS and OSDI were positively correlated at baseline (Spearman ρ = 0.547; Holm-adjusted p < 0.001) and at T5 (Spearman ρ = 0.428; Holm-adjusted p = 0.003). No treatment-related adverse events occurred. In conclusion, in TED-associated DED refractory to maximal conservative therapy, LLLT produced a significant and progressively increasing reduction in symptom burden together with an objective reduction in tear hyperosmolarity. Effects on break-up time, aqueous secretion, gland morphology, and lipid layer grade were not demonstrable within two months. The pattern and pace of response differ from those observed with the same technology after cataract surgery and are consistent with a chronic, systemically driven disease in which the ocular surface insult is continuously renewed.

Article.ArticleTitle: TNF rs1800629 Genotype and Motor Response to Intensive Rehabilitation in Parkinson's Disease: An Exploratory Study.

Abstract.AbstractText: Rehabilitation is a key component of Parkinson's disease (PD) management, although individual responses differ substantially. Genetic factors involved in neuroplasticity and inflammation may contribute to this variability. We investigated whether selected polymorphisms in inflammation- and neuroplasticity-related genes influence motor outcomes following intensive multidisciplinary rehabilitation in patients with PD. Sixty-six patients with a diagnosis of idiopathic PD were consecutively enrolled and randomly allocated to an intensive multidisciplinary rehabilitation group (EXP-Group, n = 34) or a home-based stretching control group (CTRL-Group, n = 32) for six weeks. MDS-UPDRS III score was assessed at baseline (T0) and post-treatment (T1). SNPs in the TNF, IL6, IL6R, IL1A, IL1B, IL10 and BDNF genes were genotyped. Possible associations between genotype, treatment group and MDS-UPDRS III score at T1 were analyzed using ANCOVA and linear mixed-effects models, adjusting for baseline MDS-UPDRS III score, age, sex, disease duration and levodopa equivalent daily dose (LEDD). A significant treatment group x TNF rs1800629 genotype interaction was observed (p = 0.033). Among EXP-Group patients, GG homozygotes showed lower adjusted MDS-UPDRS III scores than did the A-allele carriers (29.10 vs. 36.11; p = 0.029). Longitudinal analyses revealed a significant time × treatment group × TNF rs1800629 genotype interaction (p = 0.010), with GG homozygotes showing an approximately 10-point reduction in MDS-UPDRS III score (40.87 to 30.87; p < 0.001). These findings suggest that TNF rs1800629 contributes to variability in response to intensive multidisciplinary rehabilitation in PD.

Article.ArticleTitle: Effect of Nurse-Delivered Chlorhexidine Versus Saline Oral Care on Ventilator-Associated Events in Medical Intensive Care Patients: A Randomized Controlled Trial.

Abstract.AbstractText: To evaluate the effectiveness of nurse-delivered oral care using 0.12% chlorhexidine versus normal saline in reducing ventilator-associated events and improving clinical and oral health outcomes among adults receiving invasive mechanical ventilation in a medical intensive care unit.
Single-center, parallel-group, assessor-blinded randomized controlled trial.

Adults receiving invasive mechanical ventilation were randomly allocated to receive oral care with either 0.12% chlorhexidine or normal saline every eight hours until extubation or discharge from the ICU. The primary outcome was ventilator-associated events. Secondary outcomes included ventilator-associated pneumonia, duration of mechanical ventilation, length of stay in the intensive care unit, mortality in the intensive care unit, oral health status and intervention-related adverse events.

A total of 141 participants were randomized. No statistically significant between-group differences were observed in ventilator-associated events, ventilator-associated pneumonia, duration of mechanical ventilation, length of stay in the intensive care unit, mortality in the intensive care unit, oral health status, or intervention-related adverse events.

In this single-center superiority randomized controlled trial, nurse-delivered oral care with 0.12% chlorhexidine did not demonstrate a statistically significant reduction in ventilator-associated events compared with normal saline. Given the wide confidence intervals and lower-than-expected event rates, these findings do not confirm equivalence but suggest that routine chlorhexidine may provide limited incremental benefit over standardized mechanical oral hygiene in medical intensive care unit patients.

AbstractText.Label: IMPLICATIONS FOR THE PROFESSION AND/OR PATIENT CARE

Abstract.AbstractText: Intensive care nurses might prioritize the consistent implementation of structured, evidence-based oral care protocols. Routine use of chlorhexidine may provide limited additional benefit over normal saline in this patient population.

This study addresses the ongoing uncertainty regarding the effectiveness of chlorhexidine for routine oral care in mechanically ventilated adults. No significant differences were observed between chlorhexidine and normal saline in ventilator-associated events, clinical outcomes, oral health outcomes, or adverse events. These findings add to the growing body of evidence suggesting that the incremental benefit of chlorhexidine beyond standardized mechanical oral care may be limited and support further adequately powered multicenter trials to define its role in different intensive care populations.
This study adhered to the Consolidated Standards of Reporting Trials guideline.

ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT05913856. Available at: https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT05913856. The trial was registered after participant recruitment had commenced because of an administrative delay. No changes were made to the study design, eligibility criteria, outcomes, or analysis plan after registration.

Article.ArticleTitle: Pre-IVF lifestyle intervention and reproductive outcomes in women with overweight or obesity undergoing IVF: a randomized clinical trial.

Abstract.AbstractText: Obesity is associated with reduced female fertility and poorer in vitro fertilization (IVF) outcomes. Although pre-IVF lifestyle-based weight loss is commonly recommended for women with overweight or obesity, whether specific strategies improve reproductive outcomes remains uncertain. We compared two pre-IVF lifestyle interventions with usual care in women undergoing IVF.

In this single-center, parallel-group randomized clinical trial conducted at Shengjing Hospital of China Medical University, Shenyang, China, women aged 20-38 years with a body mass index (BMI) of 24-40 kg/m² planning IVF were randomly assigned in a 1:1:1 ratio to 12-hour time-restricted feeding plus moderate physical activity (TRF + PA), a calorie-restricted diet (CRD), or usual care. Recruitment took place from March 14, 2023, to August 20, 2024, and follow-up was completed on February 20, 2026. The primary outcome was cumulative live birth. Secondary outcomes included cumulative clinical pregnancy, miscarriage, obstetric complications, embryological outcomes, anthropometric changes, and metabolic measures.

A total of 273 women underwent randomization. Cumulative live birth did not differ between groups, occurring in 46.6% of women in the TRF + PA group, 43.8% in the CRD group, and 44.0% in the control group (P = 0.916). After adjustment for baseline waist circumference, neither intervention was associated with cumulative live birth compared with usual care (TRF + PA vs. control: adjusted risk ratio [aRR] 1.034; 95% CI, 0.746-1.434; P = 0.839; CRD vs. control: aRR 0.936; 95% CI, 0.676-1.295; P = 0.689). TRF + PA was associated with a greater reduction in homeostasis model assessment of insulin resistance (HOMA-IR) than usual care (P = 0.005). In analyses treating anthropometric change as a continuous exposure, greater reduction in body fat percentage was independently associated with a higher probability of live birth (per 1-percentage-point reduction: aRR 1.065; 95% CI, 1.021-1.111; P = 0.003). Exploratory spline analyses suggested a threshold, with higher live birth probability observed above an absolute reduction of 5.16% points in body fat percentage.

Among women with overweight or obesity undergoing IVF, pre-IVF lifestyle intervention did not improve cumulative live birth compared with usual care. However, reduction in body fat percentage was independently associated with live birth, suggesting that change in adiposity may be more relevant to reproductive outcomes than weight loss alone.

Article.ArticleTitle: Comparison of the effects of normal saline versus Plasma-Lyte® on acid-base balance during living donor kidney transplantation surgery using goal-directed fluid therapy based on pulse pressure variation- a randomised controlled trial.

Abstract.AbstractText: Normal saline (NS) is commonly used during kidney transplantation but may cause hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis when administered in large volumes. Balanced crystalloids such as Plasma-Lyte® (PL) may attenuate these effects. We compared acid-base outcomes of NS versus PL when administered using pulse pressure variation (PPV)- guided goal-directed fluid therapy during living donor kidney transplantation (LDKT).

In this prospective randomised assessor-blinded trial, adult patients undergoing LDKT were allocated to receive intraoperative NS or PL. Fluid administration was titrated according to a predefined PPV-guided algorithm. Acid-base status was assessed using the Stewart physicochemical analysis. The primary endpoint was the difference in apparent strong ion difference (SIDa). Secondary outcome measurements included haemodynamics, electrolytes, lactate, serum creatinine trends, dialysis requirement, and graft function.

A total of 111 patients were analysed (NS, n = 55, PL, n = 56). Baseline characteristics and total intraoperative fluid volumes were comparable (1796 ± 337 vs 1903 ± 434 mL; p = 0.15). Apparent strong ion difference declined over time in both groups (time effect p < 0.001), but did not differ between groups (group effect p = 0.50; interaction p = 0.37). In the baseline-adjusted analysis (ANCOVA) of the primary endpoint, the adjusted between-group difference in SIDa at the end of surgery was 0.71 mmol/L (90% CI - 0.90 to + 2.32 mmol/L) against the pre-specified equivalence margin of ± 2 mmol/L; formal equivalence was not established, although no significant difference was detected (adjusted p = 0.46). Effective strong ion difference (SID e), strong ion gap (SIG), pH, serum potassium, and lactate were similar at all measured time points (p > 0.05). Early graft dysfunction (4.1% vs 7.4%; p = 0.472) and delayed graft function (3.6% vs 0%; p = 0.150) did not differ significantly; however, the trial was not powered for these exploratory outcomes. Postoperative creatinine trajectories did not differ between groups.

During LDKT, PPV-guided goal-directed fluid therapy produced no significant between-group difference in acid-base balance or early graft outcomes with NS and PL. Formal equivalence in the primary endpoint was not established; nonetheless, at the moderate volumes delivered, the findings suggest that haemodynamic strategy may influence perioperative acid-base status more than crystalloid choice.
The study was prospectively registered in the Clinical Trials Registry of India (ctri.nic.in) Registration number: CTRI/2021/01/030227 Registered on 04/01/2021.
